title: Korsakoff Syndrome(Archived) -- Introduction
content: While there is no consensus on the actual definition of Korsakoff syndrome, it is generally agreed to be a chronic neuropsychiatric syndrome due to thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency. [1] Damage to multiple areas of the brain leads to amnesia and confusion. While classically associated with chronic alcohol use, Korsakoff syndrome can be the result of other processes that ultimately lead to thiamine deficiency. Korsakoff syndrome is most often seen in the context of chronic alcohol abuse and is thought to be on the spectrum with Wernicke encephalopathy. Wernicke encephalopathy is acute and often reversible, while Korsakoff syndrome is chronic and may be irreversible. [2] When Wernicke encephalopathy accompanies Korsakoff syndrome, it is referred to as Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Given the considerable overlap between the two diseases, this article will refer to both when evaluating and treating patients.

title: Korsakoff Syndrome(Archived) -- Etiology
content: Any condition leading to chronic thiamine deficiency can lead to Wernicke’s encephalopathy and, if untreated, to Korsakoff syndrome. [3] The most common cause of Korsakoff syndrome is chronic alcohol abuse. Alcohol interferes with the GI tract absorption of thiamine as well as with the liver's ability to store thiamine. Additionally, accompanying malnutrition often compounds the effects of alcoholism, leading to further thiamin deficiency. Other causes of Korsakoff syndrome include eating disorders, chronic vomiting (including hyperemesis gravidarum), psychiatric disorders, chemotherapy, and cancer. [4] [5]

title: Korsakoff Syndrome(Archived) -- Epidemiology
content: The worldwide prevalence of Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is thought to be between 0 and 2%. Those at higher risk include the homeless, elderly, and psychiatric patients. Because Korsakoff syndrome is grossly underdiagnosed and there is disagreement regarding precise diagnostic criteria, there is little data on the incidence and prevalence. [1]

title: Korsakoff Syndrome(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: Thiamine is an essential cofactor for multiple enzymes involved in brain cell metabolism. [6] Without these enzymes, the metabolism of multiple cell components and ATP is reduced. Thiamine is involved in pyruvate metabolism, and its deficiency can lead to elevated lactate levels, edema, neuronal loss, and reactive gliosis throughout the brain. The cognitive deficits seen in Korsakoff syndrome are thought to be primarily due to damage to the following areas: the anterior nucleus of the thalamus, mammillary bodies, and corpus callosum. [7] There is also evidence of decreased glucose metabolism in the cerebral cortex. [8] Cerebellar degeneration is also common among alcoholics and can lead to ataxia and oculomotor deficits seen in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

title: Korsakoff Syndrome(Archived) -- Histopathology
content: The most common histologic findings in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome include gliosis and microhemorrhages in the periaqueductal and paraventricular grey matter, atrophy of the mamillary bodies and thalamus, and volume deficits in the hippocampus, cerebellar hemispheres, pons, and anterior superior vermis.

title: Korsakoff Syndrome(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: As mentioned above, Wernicke encephalopathy and Korsakoff syndrome are often thought to be on a spectrum with one another as they are both due to thiamine deficiency. Thus, clinicians should screen for them together. Wernicke encephalopathy classically presents with the triad of altered mental status, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia. Less than 20% of patients will present with all three of these findings. [3] The following signs and symptoms should cause suspicion for Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome: Altered mental status (up to 82% of patients) - amnesia, disorientation, confabulations Oculomotor findings - most often horizontal nystagmus, retinal hemorrhage, ophthalmoplegia, cranial nerve IV palsy, conjugate gaze Ataxia - wide-based gait [3]

title: Korsakoff Syndrome(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: The cognitive impairments specific to Korsakoff syndrome vs Wernicke encephalopathy include anterograde amnesia, which profoundly limits learning capacity; retrograde amnesia; and executive deficits, resulting in decreased inhibition and difficulties with judgment, planning, and problem-solving. [7] Anterograde amnesia can result in the classic symptom of confabulation, in which one fills a memory gap with untrue information. [9] The Caine criteria have been described to have a sensitivity of 85% and specificity of 100% for Wernicke encephalopathy in the alcoholic population. [3] Because of the strong overlap, this can also be used to help screen for Korsakoff syndrome. Caines criteria for the diagnosis of Wernicke encephalopathy in chronic alcoholics. Two of the following 4 signs are necessary to diagnose Wernicke encephalopathy clinically: Dietary deficiency Oculomotor abnormalities Cerebellar dysfunction Either an altered mental status or mild memory impairment

title: Korsakoff Syndrome(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: Korsakoff syndrome is, for the most part, a clinical diagnosis. It should be diagnosed when the signs and symptoms described above are present in a patient with risk factors for thiamine deficiency. Thiamine blood tests often take days to result and should not delay empiric treatment. Regarding neuroimaging, CT and MRI of the brain are not often indicated for the emergent diagnosis of Korsakoff syndrome. However, they may be warranted to rule out other causes of the patient’s symptoms. Non-emergent MRI can reveal specific findings of Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, including changes in the mamillary bodies, thalami, tectal plate, and periaqueductal areas, but sensitivity is only 53%.

title: Korsakoff Syndrome(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: The mainstay of treatment in an acute presentation is thiamine replacement. There is little evidence on the amount of thiamine to replace, but typical regimens include high-dose thiamine (500-1500 mg IV) 3 times daily for at least 3 days. [3] Electrolyte abnormalities should be corrected, and fluids replaced. In particular, magnesium must be replaced, as thiamine-dependent enzymes cannot function in a magnesium-deficient state. Many patients will also need glucose replacement, and traditionally, it was thought that replacing glucose before thiamine could exacerbate the patient’s symptoms. Following a review of 19 papers, it has been recommended that hypoglycemia not be delayed. [10] Some suggestions are prolonged and not an acute replacement of glucose without thiamine supplementation, and they increase the risk of Wernicke encephalopathy. After the acute phase of vitamin and electrolyte replacement, there is mounting evidence that memory rehabilitation is beneficial in Korsakoff syndrome. Declarative memory ("knowing what") seems to be most affected in Korsakoff syndrome, leading many patients to require lifelong care. Because procedural learning ("knowing how") appears to be relatively preserved in Korsakoff syndrome, memory rehabilitation focused on this domain has shown promising outcomes. There has been some success in small Korsakoff syndrome patient populations in learning procedures and improving their autonomy. [7]

title: Korsakoff Syndrome(Archived) -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The differential diagnosis will vary depending on the patient’s presentation. Still, it may include infection, seizure, intoxication, metabolic disorders, medications, stroke, head trauma, brain mass, multiple sclerosis, migraines, vertigo, ethanol neurotoxicity, and schizophrenia. [3]

title: Korsakoff Syndrome(Archived) -- Prognosis
content: High suspicion of Wernicke’s encephalopathy is key to improving patient prognosis. Classically, the thinking was that once Korsakoff syndrome had set in, amnesia was generally irreversible. More recent research has shown promise in memory rehabilitation, including memory compensation techniques and error-less learning strategies. [1] Regarding neuroimaging, associations with cortical lesions have been shown to correlate with a worse prognosis. [3]

title: Korsakoff Syndrome(Archived) -- Consultations
content: Consultations with dietitians, social workers, neurologists, and neuropsychiatrists can be beneficial in treating Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

title: Korsakoff Syndrome(Archived) -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is vastly underdiagnosed. [3] Patients often do not present themselves due to substance abuse, and it is not until they are brought in by family members that there is an evaluation. Alcohol withdrawal and intoxication can interfere with diagnosis as well. Even once presented to the physician, it is often misdiagnosed, with one study estimating that Wernicke encephalopathy is missed in 68% of alcoholic patients and 94% of nonalcoholic patients. [3] There are also gaps in research on Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome due to a lack of a formal definition for Korsakoff syndrome, which makes it difficult to accumulate data, especially regarding epidemiology, diagnosis, and prognosis. Patients who are unable or unwilling to quit alcohol may benefit from proper nutrition and thiamine supplementation.

title: Korsakoff Syndrome(Archived) -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Korsakoff syndrome is a neuropsychiatric condition causing damage to multiple areas of the brain that results in cognitive impairment and amnesia. Korsakoff syndrome can result from any condition leading to thiamine deficiency, but it is most often seen in chronic alcohol abuse. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is a clinical diagnosis, and Wernicke encephalopathy should be suspected in anyone at risk for thiamine deficiency who presents with oculomotor findings, ataxia, or confusion. Once amnesia and executive deficits are present, Korsakoff syndrome should be suspected. The key to good outcomes is early detection of Wernicke encephalopathy and treatment with thiamine.

title: Korsakoff Syndrome(Archived) -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Providing quality care for patients with Korsakoff syndrome requires substantial resources and coordination among a variety of healthcare professionals. In the early stages, triage nurses, visiting nurses, and EMS providers can help identify patients who may present with other complaints or who would otherwise not seek care. Practical screening tools in the emergency department or outpatient clinic could help identify alcohol abuse, the major risk factor for Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. In the acute setting, identifying the disease (preferably early, before the onset of Korsakoff Syndrome) and treating it requires interprofessional collaboration among emergency physicians, neurologists, and dieticians to rule out other causes and provide appropriate treatment. Long-term care of these patients may require the attention of neuropsychiatrists, neurologists, psychiatrists, dieticians, social workers, and the patient’s primary care provider to ensure sobriety, continued nutrition, and memory rehabilitation.
